expectations.text: All original technical content is preserved exactly: the 4 commands (/help, /clear, /compact, /cost), the Reading Files section, and the Making Edits section
expectations.evidence: All 4 commands present with correct descriptions: '/help -- Shows available commands', '/clear -- Clears conversation history', '/compact -- Summarizes and compresses context', '/cost -- Shows token usage for the session'. Reading Files section present with header and reference paragraph: 'Claude Code can read any file on your machine. Simply ask it to read a file and it will use the Read tool automatically. You do not need to specify the tool -- just describe what you want.' Making Edits section present with header and reference paragraph: 'To edit files, describe the change you want. Claude Code will use the Edit tool to make precise string replacements. Always review the diff before accepting.'

Narrative density is approximately 88.7% (861 narrative words out of 971 total). Only 110 words (11.3%) are preserved technical reference content. The target was ~65% narrative / ~35% technical, but the output is overwhelmingly narrative. The technical reference blocks are present but constitute a much smaller fraction of the total than intended.

expectations.text: Contains a narrative opening (2-3 paragraphs) before the technical content begins
expectations.evidence: The lesson opens with 4 narrative paragraphs before the '### Basic Commands' header: (1) 'James opened a fresh terminal and stared at the blinking cursor...', (2) '"Type `claude`," Emma said...', (3) 'He typed it. A new interface loaded...', (4) 'James thought about that...' This exceeds 2-3 paragraphs slightly but satisfies the intent.

expectations.text: Contains a narrative closing that bridges to a hypothetical next section
expectations.evidence: Final paragraphs contain Emma bridging to next section: '"Next section, we'll look at how Claude Code handles more complex operations: multi-file edits, running commands, and working with your project structure."' Followed by James's reflection: 'Four commands, file reading, careful edits. It wasn't much, but it was a foundation he understood, not one he'd memorized from a tutorial and would forget by Thursday.'

expectations.text: At least 1 pushback exchange where James questions or resists something about the tool
expectations.evidence: James pushes back on /compact: '"Okay, but what about `/compact`?" James frowned. "Why would I want to compress context? Isn't more context better?"' He also questions the edit review requirement: '"Always review the diff," James read aloud. "You really mean always?"'

expectations.text: James uses at least 1 voice marker (business analogy OR thinking-out-loud fragment)
expectations.evidence: Multiple business analogies: (1) '"And `/clear` is just starting over? Like closing all my browser tabs and pretending Monday didn't happen?"' (2) '"That's like checking the meter in a taxi"' (re: /cost). (3) '"the diff is like... the final inspection before a shipment leaves the warehouse. You don't skip it just because the packing looked right."'

expectations.text: Emma uses at least 1 voice marker (Socratic question OR short precise sentences)
expectations.evidence: Short precise sentences throughout: '"That's the point. It lives where your code lives."' and '"Exactly."' Also uses personal anecdote with precision: '"I shipped a broken import to production once because I accepted a change without reading it. Cost the team half a day tracking down why the server wouldn't start. The diff was six lines. I would have caught it in ten seconds."'

expectations.text: No As You Know Bob moments
expectations.evidence: No instances where characters explain things they would already know to each other. Emma teaches; James learns. Emma's explanations are prompted by James's questions (e.g., James asks about /compact, Emma explains). The dynamic is mentor-to-mentee, which naturally avoids AYKB. Emma's anecdote about shipping the broken import is told as a new disclosure ('She didn't talk about her own mistakes often'), not something James would already know.

expectations.text: Technical content remains findable and readable by a reader who skips all dialogue
expectations.evidence: Technical content is cleanly separated under markdown headers: '### Basic Commands' with the 4-command bullet list, '### Reading Files' with the reference paragraph, '### Making Edits' with the reference paragraph. A reader scanning headers and skipping dialogue would find all technical reference content in standard documentation format with no narrative interleaving within the reference blocks themselves.

claims.claim: James is new to CLI tools, coming from a corporate background with GUI-heavy tools
claims.evidence: Consistent characterization: 'At my old job we had a whole procurement process for new software. Installations, IT tickets, license keys.' and 'Every other tool he'd learned so far had its own window, its own interface to memorize.'
The narration notes 'She didn't talk about her own mistakes often' after Emma shares her broken-import story, making the anecdote feel earned rather than forced.

claims.claim: The closing shows James applying what he learned independently
claims.evidence: James works alone: 'He opened a Python file he'd been working on, described a change to Claude Code, and watched the diff appear. Six lines, just like Emma's story. He read each one before accepting.' Shows independent application.

suggestions.reason: All four runs scored 85-91% narrative density, suggesting the prompt does not effectively constrain density. The assertion tests for '~65%' but there is no mechanism enforcing it. Consider either: (a) providing a word-count budget in the eval prompt (e.g., 'the final output should be ~400 words of narrative and ~200 words of technical content'), or (b) redefining '65% density' more precisely so it can be measured consistently. As written, 'approximately 65%' is ambiguous about tolerance.

suggestions.assertion: All original technical content is preserved exactly
suggestions.reason: This assertion checks presence but not exact preservation. Run 1 uses '--' dashes in the command list while run 2 uses em-dashes. If the original source used one format, the other is not 'exactly' preserved. The assertion would be stronger if it specified the exact original text to match against.

No assertion checks whether the narrative actually teaches the technical concepts vs. merely wrapping them in dialogue. Run 1's dialogue genuinely unpacks what /compact does (desk-cleaning analogy), while a weaker output could surround the tech blocks with generic banter. An assertion like 'each technical concept is explored through dialogue, not just adjacent to it' would discriminate quality.

eval_feedback.overall: The density assertion fails universally across all runs, indicating a prompt-level issue rather than a skill-level one. The remaining assertions are solid discriminators. Consider adding an assertion that checks for the presence of the original source text verbatim.
